screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn to find the true cause of slow systems by focusing on the key resources every Linux host uses: C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network input and output. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to gather evidence, avoid premature optimization, and pick targeted fixes with confidence. Think of this as a troubleshooting recipe: observe, measure, identify, change, and verify. Which resource will you check first when a server slows down?

screens.title: First triage with top and htop
screens.narratorSegment: When a system becomes slow, the fastest way to gather evidence is to run a live process viewer. Top and htop give a near-instant snapshot of which processes consume C P U and memory, along with system-wide summary lines. Start with top to see the C P U line, memory totals, swap usage, and the load average. The load average shows the average number of processes in the run queue over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; if these numbers consistently exceed the number of C P U cores, that signals a C P U-bound system. Watch the wa value in the C P U line; a high wa means the C P U is spending time waiting for disk input and output. Htop offers a friendlier display with colorful meters and easier process selection, useful when you want to send signals or sort by different columns quickly. A concrete example: if top shows one process using 95% C P U and load equals cores, that's a C P U issue; if C P U usage is low but wa is 60%, you're likely hitting disk input and output. A common mistake is to chase a single high process without checking if multiple processes collectively overload memory or input and output. After observing, collect a short sample, then move to vmstat or iostat to confirm the resource in question. How will you validate a suspected bottleneck after this quick check?

keyIdea.title: Triage principle
keyIdea.text: Use top/htop to form an initial hypothesis: CPU bound, memory pressure, or I/O wait, then confirm with specialized tools.

content.html:
Core Concept
First triage with top and htop
Form a working hypothesis about the resource under stress.
Sample top-like summary (annotated)
PID USER PR NI VIRT RES SHR S %CPU %MEM TIME+ COMMAND 1234 dbuser 20 0 1.2g 500m 20m R 95.0 30.0 120:45 mysqld %Cpu(s): 5.0 us, 2.0 sy, 0.0 ni, 92.0 id, 1.0 wa Mem: 32G total, 8G used, 24G free, 1G buffers Swap: 0B total, 0B used Load average: 3.50, 3.20, 2.80 Annotations: - High %CPU on mysqld => likely CPU-bound if load ~ cores. - wa (I/O wait) would point to disk latency if large.
Key Takeaway
Top gives immediate clues; don't act before confirming with vmstat or iostat.
Common mistake
Killing a high CPU process without understanding its role can cause outages.
Practice steps
  1. Run top or htop and note CPU, wa, load average, memory and swap.
  2. Identify top processes by %CPU and %MEM; note PIDs for later inspection.
  3. If wa is high or load >> cores, capture vmstat and iostat samples to confirm.
Check your understanding
If CPU usage is low but wa is 60%, which resource is likely the bottleneck? Think of why adding RAM would not help here.

screens.title: Understanding load average and I/O wait
screens.narratorSegment: Two numbers you will encounter repeatedly are the load average and the input and output wait percentage. Load average shows how many processes are in the run queue over time; it is not a percent but a count. If your 1, 5 and 15 minute averages are consistently above the number of C P U cores, that's a sign the C P U is overloaded. Contrast that with wa, which appears on the C P U summary and indicates the percentage of C P U time spent waiting for input and output to complete. A high wa often accompanies a disk bottleneck: processes are runnable but blocked because reads or writes are slow. For example, a 4‑core machine with load average 8.0 means twice as many runnable processes as cores — a C P U issue. But if the C P U line shows 95% idle and wa at 60%, the C P U is idle waiting on disk, so adding C P U won't help. A common misconception is treating low C P U usage as absence of performance problems; it may hide input and output waits or memory pressure. Your next steps should be to run vmstat and iostat to confirm whether the subsystem causing waits is disk or swap, then plan a targeted remediation.

keyIdea.title: Interpretation rule
keyIdea.text: Load average > CPU cores suggests CPU contention; high wa with idle CPU suggests an I/O disk bottleneck.

content.html:
Definition
Load average vs I/O wait
Understand the numeric meaning and practical implications for troubleshooting.
Quick comparison
Load average
Average runnable processes over time. Compare to CPU core count.
I/O wait (wa)
Percent of CPU time waiting for I/O. High values point to disk or storage latency.
Key Takeaway

Always compare load average to the number of cores and verify high wa with iostat or vmstat before changing hardware.

Example scenario
A 4-core VM shows load averages 6.2, 5.8, 5.0 and %Cpu(s): 5 us, 2 sy, 92 id, 1 wa. Here, load > cores but CPU is mostly idle. The explanation is blocked processes waiting on disk or swap, making the run queue longer while CPU remains idle waiting for I/O. Resolve by measuring disk latency and queue depth with iostat.
Misconception check
Don't assume low user CPU means healthy: idle time can hide long I/O waits. Always corroborate multiple metrics.

screens.title: Memory signals: free, vmstat, and swapping
screens.narratorSegment: Memory pressure differs from C P U and disk problems because it affects how often the kernel moves pages between R A M and swap. Use free -h for a quick snapshot of total, used, free and swap, but rely on vmstat for trend information. Running vmstat with a one second interval gives you continuous samples showing processes, memory, page in/out, block input and output and C P U activity. In vmstat output, si and so represent swap in and swap out; consistent non‑zero values indicate active swapping. Swapping slows performance dramatically because disk access is orders of magnitude slower than R A M. For example, if vmstat shows si=50 and so=30 consistently while C P U idle remains low, your system is thrashing between R A M and swap and needs more physical memory or fewer active memory consumers. A common mistake is to immediately add swap; swap can be a temporary relief but does not replace required R A M for sustained workloads. Always look for the root cause of memory pressure — runaway processes, memory leaks, or workload demands — before resizing instances or adding R A M.

keyIdea.title: Memory rule
keyIdea.text: Non-zero si/so in vmstat means active swapping; swapping degrades performance and often requires adding RAM or reducing memory consumption.

content.html:
Definition
Memory signals and swapping
When the system moves pages to swap, performance typically drops sharply.
$ free -h total used free shared buff/cache available Mem: 32G 20G 8G 512M 4G 11G Swap: 4G 1G 3G $ vmstat 1 5 procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu----- r b swpd free buff cache si so bi bo in cs us sy id wa 1 0 1048576 8388608 1024 4194304 50 30 0 10 100 200 30 10 40 20
Key Takeaway
Consistent si/so values mean active swapping; increasing RAM or reducing memory usage is needed.
Concrete example
A web server serving many large in-memory caches may push a VM into swap during peak traffic. Check vmstat si/so; if swap activity is frequent, reduce cache size or increase RAM.
Misconception
Swap presence alone is not always bad; brief swap use is acceptable. It's the sustained, frequent swap activity that causes thrashing and visible slowdowns.

screens.title: Investigating disk I/O with iostat
screens.narratorSegment: Disk input and output problems are frequent and can be detected with iostat. The extended iostat output includes per-device metrics such as reads per second, writes per second, read KB/s, write KB/s, %util (percentage of time the device was busy), await (average latency) and svctm (average service time). A device with %util near 100% is a clear sign it's saturated. High await and svctm values point to slow device response. For example, running iostat -x 1 will show live changes: if %util is persistently 95 to 100 and await is high, processes waiting for disk cause system-wide slowdowns and high wa in top. Also consider the nature of input and output: databases typically generate random input and output and suffer more from high latency, while backup jobs are sequential and more sensitive to bandwidth. A common error is treating overall throughput numbers without considering queue depth and average wait time; throughput may look acceptable while latency kills performance. After identifying the busy device, inspect queue depth, filesystem health, or storage layer metrics, and consider moving hot data to faster storage or optimizing the workload.

keyIdea.title: iostat insight
keyIdea.text: Persistent %util near 100% and high await indicate a disk I/O bottleneck that requires storage or workload changes.

content.html:
Process Flow
Investigating disk I/O with iostat
Device-level stats reveal whether the storage layer is the bottleneck.
$ iostat -x 1 3 Device: rrqm/s wrqm/s r/s w/s rkB/s wkB/s avgrq-sz avgqu-sz await svctm %util sda 0.00 0.50 10.00 50.00 400.0 1024.0 30.0 1.20 25.0 5.00 95.00
Interpretation: %util 95% suggests the disk is busy almost all the time. await 25 ms and avgqu-sz > 1 indicate queueing and latency that slow processes down.
Pro Tip
Differentiate sequential vs random I/O. Databases suffer more from latency than backups.
Common mistake
Relying only on throughput without checking latency and queue size can miss real problems.
Step checklist
  1. Run iostat -x 1 to collect samples over time.
  2. Observe %util, await, svctm and avgqu-sz for each device.
  3. If %util near 100% and high await, plan to reduce load, migrate hot data, or improve storage performance.
Key Takeaway
Device-level metrics expose storage saturation; address latency and queueing, not just throughput.

screens.title: Diagnosing network I/O issues
screens.narratorSegment: Network problems often involve components outside the box, but local statistics can reveal many issues. Use ss -s to get socket statistics and sar -n DEV 1 to sample interface-level metrics like received/transmitted packets and kilobytes per second. Look for increasing rxkB/s or txkB/s that match expected traffic, but watch for rxerr or txerr values — rising errors or drops indicate physical issues, faulty drivers, or saturated interfaces. Ping and traceroute remain useful to check basic latency and path issues between hosts. A concrete troubleshooting flow: confirm the application is sending expected traffic, run sar -n DEV to see interface load, use ss to check large numbers of connections or sockets in a wait state, and run ping/traceroute to determine if latency or routing causes the slowdown. Remember that saturated interfaces may require traffic shaping, additional interfaces, or network team involvement. A common misconception is to blame the server when the problem sits in a switch, router, or upstream link; local metrics help you gather evidence to engage networking teams with confidence. Diagnosing network I/O issues means interface errors, drops, or unusual packet rates in sar or ss suggest network-level problems that may need external investigation.. In practical terms, use ss, sar and basic network tools to detect local network stress. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Interface errors, drops, or unusual packet rates in sar or ss suggest network-level problems that may need external investigation.

content.html:
Comparison
Network diagnostics with ss and sar
Build evidence for local interface issues before blaming application code.
$ ss -s Total: 100 (established 40, closed 30, orphaned 0, synrecv 0, timewait 20) $ sar -n DEV 1 3 IFACE rxpck/s txpck/s rxkB/s txkB/s rxerr/s txerr/s eth0 200 180 1024.0 900.0 0.00 0.00
Interpretation: watch for growing timewait counts, err packets, or drops. Rising rxerr/txerr suggests hardware or driver problems; rising packet rates with drops may indicate saturation.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm expected traffic patterns for the application.
  • Run sar -n DEV to capture interface stats and compare to baseline.
  • Use ss to inspect connection states and counts for anomalies.
  • Use ping/traceroute to check latency and routing.
Key Takeaway
Local network counters can prove whether a problem is on the host or upstream, enabling informed escalation.

screens.title: Establish baselines and avoid premature optimization
screens.narratorSegment: A baseline is a record of what normal operation looks like for your system. Without it, you cannot tell if current metrics are unusual or expected. Building a baseline means sampling the same metrics during representative workloads and storing those results for comparison. Use vmstat, iostat, and sar run with fixed intervals to capture several minutes of activity and save the outputs. For example, schedule sar -u and sar -n DEV during business hours and compare it to overnight traffic patterns. Baselines help you detect deviations, seasonal load patterns, and the difference between a spike and sustained overload. The classic mistake is changing configuration or hardware based on one snapshot. Instead follow this process: collect evidence, form a hypothesis, change one variable, then remeasure. This approach avoids chasing symptoms and wasting resources. A final point: when automating collection, keep timestamps and host identifiers so that later you can correlate events across machines and times of day. Establish baselines and avoid premature optimization means collect representative, timestamped samples to know what 'normal' looks like; always compare anomalies to your baseline before acting.. In practical terms, why a baseline matters and how to collect meaningful normal-state samples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Baseline principle
keyIdea.text: Collect representative, timestamped samples to know what 'normal' looks like; always compare anomalies to your baseline before acting.

content.html:
Process Flow
Establish baselines
Collect metrics routinely and compare anomalies to normal behavior.
  1. Choose representative times and intervals (e.g., vmstat 1 300 for 5 minutes).
  2. Collect CPU, memory, disk and network samples and tag them with host and timestamp.
  3. Store outputs centrally for trend comparison and alerting thresholds.
Key Takeaway
A one-off sample is rarely enough; baselines turn noisy numbers into meaningful signals.
Example schedule
Run vmstat 1 300 and iostat -x 1 300 during peak and off-peak hours, store files with host and timestamp and compare averages and percentiles across days.
Pitfall
Avoid immediate hardware changes based on a single spike; confirm with baseline data and repeated samples first.

screens.title: Automating metric collection with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible is a practical tool to run the same measurement commands across many hosts and collect outputs centrally. The chapter includes a template playbook that runs date, vmstat and iostat, then delegates saving the outputs to the control node with host and timestamp prefixes. Automation gives you consistent formatting, repeatable sampling, and easier comparison across a cluster. When writing such playbooks, mark commands as changed_when: false to avoid noisy change reports, and use run_once for control-node directory creation. The saved logs should include the hostname and a timestamp so you can correlate samples across hosts. Automate with Ansible
Run the same commands on all relevant hosts and save outputs centrally with clear file names.
--- - name: Monitor Database Server Performance hosts: dbservers become: yes tasks: - name: Get current timestamp command: date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S register: current_timestamp changed_when: false - name: Gather vmstat output shell: vmstat 1 5 register: vmstat_output changed_when: false - name: Gather iostat output shell: iostat -x 1 5 register: iostat_output changed_when: false - name: Create performance reports directory delegate_to: localhost file: path: "./performance_reports/{{ inventory_hostname }}" state: directory run_once: true - name: Save vmstat output to file delegate_to: localhost copy: content: | VMStat Output for {{ inventory_hostname }} at {{ current_timestamp.stdout }}: ------------------------------------------------------------------ {{ vmstat_output.stdout }} dest: "./performance_reports/{{ inventory_hostname }}/vmstat_{{ current_timestamp.stdout }}.log" when: vmstat_output is defined

Assessment
Interpret outputs — examples
Use metric evidence to answer diagnostic questions concisely.
Question 1
Top shows wa > 50% regularly. What is the primary bottleneck?
Answer: Disk I/O. High wa means CPU waits for I/O; target storage latency or queueing.
Question 2
vmstat shows consistent si and so activity. What does that imply?
Answer: Active swapping and memory pressure; add RAM or reduce memory usage and re-measure.
Write a diagnostic note
Observed: iostat %util ~98% and await 40ms. Diagnosis: storage device saturated causing high latency and process waits. Immediate action: move hot files to faster storage or reduce I/O during peak. Re-measure: run iostat -x 1 60 before and after the change to compare await and %util.
Key Takeaway
Answer diagnostics by citing metrics, providing a targeted remediation, and specifying how to verify the result.

screens.title: From evidence to action: a safe remediation checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've identified a probable bottleneck, follow a disciplined remediation checklist: make one targeted change, measure its effect, and then decide on next steps. Start with the least disruptive option: adjust application configuration (for example reduce cache size or change backup schedules). If that fails, consider scaling vertically or horizontally, or improving storage. Always document what you changed and when. For instance, if disk latency causes high wa, you might reschedule heavy backups, move hot tables to faster disks, or increase IOPS on the storage tier. After a change, rerun the same vmstat, iostat or sar samples you used to diagnose the problem and compare against your baseline. This gives you evidence that the change helped or not. A common error is making multiple changes at once because that prevents you from knowing which action produced the result. By applying a single change and remeasuring, you learn what truly helps and build reproducible fixes. What will be the first minimal change you try next time you detect a disk bottleneck? From evidence to action: a safe remediation checklist means change one variable at a time and remeasure with the same sampling commands to verify whether the fix worked.. In practical terms, one targeted change at a time, then remeasure — the safest path to improved performance. Best Practice
From evidence to action
A safe checklist to implement changes with confidence.
  1. Document baseline metrics and timestamp before changes.
  2. Pick one targeted, reversible change.
  3. Apply change during a controlled window.
  4. Rerun identical measurements and compare to baseline.
Key Takeaway
Single, reversible changes with before/after measurements create reliable, learnable operations.
Example actions by bottleneck
  • CPU bound: profile processes, reduce concurrency, or scale CPU resources.
  • Memory pressure: reduce caches, fix leaks, or add RAM.
  • Disk I/O: reschedule jobs, move hot data, or increase storage performance.
After any change, run the same iostat/vmstat/sar samples used originally to confirm whether the measured symptom improved.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn to find the true cause of slow systems by focusing on the key resources every Linux host uses: C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network input and output. We'll introduce the standard, built‑in tools you will use every day — top and htop for a quick health check, vmstat and free for memory signals, iostat for disk behavior, and sar for historical sampling. You will also practice interpreting the numbers these tools show so you can distinguish between symptoms and root causes. For example, high C P U utilization looks very different from heavy swapping or a saturated disk, and the right fix depends on that distinction. Finally, you'll see how Ansible can automate metric collection so you can compare hosts and build a baseline. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to gather evidence, avoid premature optimization, and pick targeted fixes with confidence. Think of this as a troubleshooting recipe: observe, measure, identify, change, and verify. Which resource will you check first when a server slows down?

By the end of this chapter you should be able to identify where a system is constrained, use the standard Linux tools to collect the right evidence, interpret those results to find a root cause, and automate basic data collection. First, you will learn to recognize C P U, memory, disk and network bottlenecks and why each one matters for application behavior. Next, you'll master the practical commands — top and htop for live process visibility, vmstat and free for memory signals, and iostat for disk metrics. Then you'll practice interpreting the numbers: what a high wait input and output percentage means, or what non‑zero swap activity implies. Finally, you'll apply Ansible to run these commands across several hosts and gather logs for later comparison. These skills let you move from guesswork to targeted fixes, making your troubleshooting faster and less risky. Build a habit of measuring before changing, and you'll avoid common mistakes like adding memory when the C P U is the real constraint.

This second objectives page focuses on how you will practice and demonstrate your skills. You will run live commands under simulated load and learn to read their output reliably — for example, recognizing high wa in top as a disk symptom or non‑zero si/so in vmstat as memory pressure. You will practice collecting multiple samples with iostat and sar so you can spot sustained trends versus temporary spikes. Then you'll put that into an Ansible playbook that gathers vmstat and iostat output from a dbservers group and stores logs with timestamps. Your assessment will be scenario based: given sample output, you will identify the most likely bottleneck and explain the evidence. Finally, you'll learn the common pitfall: applying a change before you have proof. That habit separates reactive admins from confident troubleshooting professionals. Practice the sequence: measure, hypothesize, change one thing, and remeasure.

When a system becomes slow, the fastest way to gather evidence is to run a live process viewer. Top and htop give a near-instant snapshot of which processes consume C P U and memory, along with system-wide summary lines. Start with top to see the C P U line, memory totals, swap usage, and the load average. The load average shows the average number of processes in the run queue over 1, 5 and 15 minutes; if these numbers consistently exceed the number of C P U cores, that signals a C P U-bound system. Watch the wa value in the C P U line; a high wa means the C P U is spending time waiting for disk input and output. Htop offers a friendlier display with colorful meters and easier process selection, useful when you want to send signals or sort by different columns quickly. A concrete example: if top shows one process using 95% C P U and load equals cores, that's a C P U issue; if C P U usage is low but wa is 60%, you're likely hitting disk input and output. A common mistake is to chase a single high process without checking if multiple processes collectively overload memory or input and output. After observing, collect a short sample, then move to vmstat or iostat to confirm the resource in question. How will you validate a suspected bottleneck after this quick check?

Two numbers you will encounter repeatedly are the load average and the input and output wait percentage. Load average shows how many processes are in the run queue over time; it is not a percent but a count. If your 1, 5 and 15 minute averages are consistently above the number of C P U cores, that's a sign the C P U is overloaded. Contrast that with wa, which appears on the C P U summary and indicates the percentage of C P U time spent waiting for input and output to complete. A high wa often accompanies a disk bottleneck: processes are runnable but blocked because reads or writes are slow. For example, a 4‑core machine with load average 8.0 means twice as many runnable processes as cores — a C P U issue. But if the C P U line shows 95% idle and wa at 60%, the C P U is idle waiting on disk, so adding C P U won't help. A common misconception is treating low C P U usage as absence of performance problems; it may hide input and output waits or memory pressure. Your next steps should be to run vmstat and iostat to confirm whether the subsystem causing waits is disk or swap, then plan a targeted remediation.

Memory pressure differs from C P U and disk problems because it affects how often the kernel moves pages between R A M and swap. Use free -h for a quick snapshot of total, used, free and swap, but rely on vmstat for trend information. Running vmstat with a one second interval gives you continuous samples showing processes, memory, page in/out, block input and output and C P U activity. In vmstat output, si and so represent swap in and swap out; consistent non‑zero values indicate active swapping. Swapping slows performance dramatically because disk access is orders of magnitude slower than R A M. For example, if vmstat shows si=50 and so=30 consistently while C P U idle remains low, your system is thrashing between R A M and swap and needs more physical memory or fewer active memory consumers. A common mistake is to immediately add swap; swap can be a temporary relief but does not replace required R A M for sustained workloads. Always look for the root cause of memory pressure — runaway processes, memory leaks, or workload demands — before resizing instances or adding R A M.

Disk input and output problems are frequent and can be detected with iostat. The extended iostat output includes per-device metrics such as reads per second, writes per second, read KB/s, write KB/s, %util (percentage of time the device was busy), await (average latency) and svctm (average service time). A device with %util near 100% is a clear sign it's saturated. High await and svctm values point to slow device response. For example, running iostat -x 1 will show live changes: if %util is persistently 95 to 100 and await is high, processes waiting for disk cause system-wide slowdowns and high wa in top. Also consider the nature of input and output: databases typically generate random input and output and suffer more from high latency, while backup jobs are sequential and more sensitive to bandwidth. A common error is treating overall throughput numbers without considering queue depth and average wait time; throughput may look acceptable while latency kills performance. After identifying the busy device, inspect queue depth, filesystem health, or storage layer metrics, and consider moving hot data to faster storage or optimizing the workload.

Network problems often involve components outside the box, but local statistics can reveal many issues. Use ss -s to get socket statistics and sar -n DEV 1 to sample interface-level metrics like received/transmitted packets and kilobytes per second. Look for increasing rxkB/s or txkB/s that match expected traffic, but watch for rxerr or txerr values — rising errors or drops indicate physical issues, faulty drivers, or saturated interfaces. Ping and traceroute remain useful to check basic latency and path issues between hosts. A concrete troubleshooting flow: confirm the application is sending expected traffic, run sar -n DEV to see interface load, use ss to check large numbers of connections or sockets in a wait state, and run ping/traceroute to determine if latency or routing causes the slowdown. Remember that saturated interfaces may require traffic shaping, additional interfaces, or network team involvement. A common misconception is to blame the server when the problem sits in a switch, router, or upstream link; local metrics help you gather evidence to engage networking teams with confidence. Diagnosing network I/O issues means interface errors, drops, or unusual packet rates in sar or ss suggest network-level problems that may need external investigation.. In practical terms, use ss, sar and basic network tools to detect local network stress. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A baseline is a record of what normal operation looks like for your system. Without it, you cannot tell if current metrics are unusual or expected. Building a baseline means sampling the same metrics during representative workloads and storing those results for comparison. Use vmstat, iostat, and sar run with fixed intervals to capture several minutes of activity and save the outputs. For example, schedule sar -u and sar -n DEV during business hours and compare it to overnight traffic patterns. Baselines help you detect deviations, seasonal load patterns, and the difference between a spike and sustained overload. The classic mistake is changing configuration or hardware based on one snapshot. Instead follow this process: collect evidence, form a hypothesis, change one variable, then remeasure. This approach avoids chasing symptoms and wasting resources. A final point: when automating collection, keep timestamps and host identifiers so that later you can correlate events across machines and times of day. This assessment-style lesson helps you practice interpretation. First example: top shows wa consistently above 50%. Which resource is likely the primary bottleneck? High wa points to disk input and output, because the C P U spends time waiting for input and output operations to complete. Second example: vmstat shows non-zero si and so values across samples. That indicates active swapping and memory pressure, which degrades performance. When answering these questions, explain which metric led you to the conclusion and why alternatives are less likely. For instance, high wa rules out pure C P U saturation; adding R A M won't help a disk-saturated system. Another useful habit is to name the corrective action you would try first and the measurement you would rerun to verify impact. Once you've identified a probable bottleneck, follow a disciplined remediation checklist: make one targeted change, measure its effect, and then decide on next steps. Start with the least disruptive option: adjust application configuration (for example reduce cache size or change backup schedules). If that fails, consider scaling vertically or horizontally, or improving storage. Always document what you changed and when. For instance, if disk latency causes high wa, you might reschedule heavy backups, move hot tables to faster disks, or increase IOPS on the storage tier. After a change, rerun the same vmstat, iostat or sar samples you used to diagnose the problem and compare against your baseline. This gives you evidence that the change helped or not. A common error is making multiple changes at once because that prevents you from knowing which action produced the result. By applying a single change and remeasuring, you learn what truly helps and build reproducible fixes. What will be the first minimal change you try next time you detect a disk bottleneck? From evidence to action: a safe remediation checklist means change one variable at a time and remeasure with the same sampling commands to verify whether the fix worked.. Remember these core concepts as you diagnose system slowdowns. C P U bottlenecks occur when C P U utilization and load average exceed available cores, indicating compute contention. Memory bottlenecks surface as active swapping in vmstat's si/so values, which hurt performance because swap uses disk. Disk input and output bottlenecks are identified by high iostat %util and elevated await and avg queue sizes, signaling storage saturation. Network issues show up as interface errors, drops, or unexpected packet patterns in sar and ss. Use these concise clues to form an initial hypothesis, then confirm with repeatable samples. These core ideas will guide your next steps and help you avoid chasing the wrong resource. Keep these tool associations and the troubleshooting loop in mind. top and htop give you immediate process and summary lines; watch wa and load averages there. vmstat and free reveal real memory behavior and swapping; si/so values are direct indicators of swap activity. iostat exposes device-level read/write rates, %util and await, which are essential for diagnosing storage issues. sar can sample and save historical C P U, input and output and network stats, making baselines and trend analysis possible. The troubleshooting loop remains the same: observe metrics, hypothesize a cause, make one targeted change, and remeasure using the same commands. Automation with Ansible collects consistent evidence across hosts, aiding comparison and trend identification. These small habits make system diagnosis faster, more accurate, and less risky in production environments.
